title: Kickoff and agenda
gist: Asher frames the goal: leave with Q4 priorities the team believes in, given roughly 11 engineers of capacity, and lays out the agenda.

turns.t: Okay, I think — is that everyone? I see Maya, Daniel, Priya. Kenji, hi. Ravi. Sofia's here. Tom's — Tom said he's two minutes out, he's coming off a call with Harbor & Pine, so let's just start and he can catch up.
Hi. Hello.
Works for me.
Can you hear me okay? I switched headsets, this one's been kind of flaky.
You're good. A little quiet, but good.
Okay. Better?

Better. So, okay. Thanks everyone for doing this on a Friday afternoon, I know for some of you it's the last meeting of the week and you'd rather be anywhere else. The goal today is simple to say and hard to do. We have to leave this call with Q4 priorities that we actually believe in. Not a wish list. And the constraint is capacity. Maya and I went through it on Wednesday and it's about eleven engineers, call it eleven, for the quarter, and that's before holidays and on-call eat into it.

Eleven-ish. Eleven is generous, honestly. Once you take out on-call, Thanksgiving week, and the December freeze starting the 14th, it's more like nine and a half engineers of actual building time. And most of that is already spoken for by v3 GA. I'll get into the math when we hit the trade-offs, but I want everyone walking in knowing it's tight.

Which is exactly why we're doing this as one meeting and not five separate ones. So, the agenda. First, ten minutes or less on Q3, where we landed. Then Routing v3 GA scope, because that's the thing we've committed to and the date's not moving. Then the — the stuff that's competing for whatever's left. Live ETA sharing, driver onboarding, and Ravi's reliability follow-ups from the outage. Then we make the call, and then OKRs and owners. I'd like us to actually decide things today. If we walk out with 'let's take it offline' on everything, I've failed.
Hey, sorry, sorry — I'm here. What did I miss?
Nothing yet. You're right on time for the part where I say we're deciding things today.
Great. Love that. Love deciding things.
He says that now.
I say it every time, Sofia.

Okay, one ground rule. The docs are all in the folder — the capacity sheet, the beta report, Priya's onboarding funnel. I'm not going to screen-share all of them. If you need a number, ask, and whoever owns it answers. Cool? Okay. Maya, do you want to do the Q3 numbers or should I?
You start, I'll jump in.

title: Q3 in review
gist: Routing v3 beta beat its targets (11% fewer miles, on-time 91.2% to 94.6%), Ravi recaps the Sep 24 outage and late status page, Sofia relays Brightside's frustration, and Tom says pipeline is strong with Harbor & Pine as the big deal.

turns.t: So, Q3. The headline is Routing v3 beta. We've had six fleets on it since September 8th, and the results are honestly better than I expected. Eleven percent fewer miles driven — that's across all six, weighted — and on-time delivery went from 91.2 to 94.6 percent. Which, for context, the target we set back in the spring was 93.
That's the slide. That's the slide I want in every deck.

And it's held up, which is the part I care about. It's not like week one was great and then it decayed. Week four was actually the best week. On the engineering side, quick scorecard. We shipped the solver migration, the beta rollout tooling, and the new dispatch board filters. What slipped was the CSV import rewrite, about three weeks, mostly because we pulled two people onto beta support when the second beta fleet had that whole depot geocoding mess. I'd make that trade again. But it's why I'm allergic to anything unplanned this quarter. Every time we've said it's just a couple of weeks this year, it's been double.
It has been double. I have the receipts.
He does have the receipts.

One caveat, small one. The eleven percent is miles, not time. Drive-time savings are more like eight, eight and a half, because the solver is happy to take a slightly slower road if it saves distance. Nobody's complained. But if sales says 'eleven percent faster,' that's wrong.
Noted. Fewer miles, not faster. Got it.
And part of the on-time number is the ETA model. Mean absolute error went from 6.1 to 4.3 minutes on the beta fleets. I'll talk about where it's still bad later.

Yeah, let's save that for GA scope. And good catch, Daniel, on miles versus time. Okay, and then the not-great part of Q3. Ravi, can you do the short version of the 24th? Short version — we did the long version in the retro.

Yeah. So Thursday, September 24th, the ETA service was down for forty-seven minutes, 14:12 to 14:59 UTC. Root cause: the Redis cluster did a failover, which on its own should've been a blip, but the dispatch workers all retried at once — no backoff, no jitter — and that retry storm knocked the ETA service over. Three hundred and twelve fleets affected. Drivers saw stale ETAs and end customers got wrong delivery windows. And — I'll just say it — the status page was updated twenty-six minutes in. That's on us. That's on me, really.
It's on the process, not just you.
Sure, but right now I'm the process. Anyway. I've got follow-ups, I'll get to them in the reliability section.

Can I add the customer side for a second? Because Brightside was the loudest one. Jordan called me directly, which he doesn't do. Their drivers were staring at ETAs that were forty minutes old, and their customers got texts saying 'arriving 2:15' for orders that showed up at three-something. Groceries. Ice cream melting, the whole thing. And Aisha, their fleet manager, told me her dispatch team was refreshing our status page and it said 'all systems operational' for almost half an hour. That's the part that stung.
Yeah. Yeah, that's fair.

And — this matters for later — Jordan, on that same call, brought up live ETA sharing again. That's the second time he's asked. He said, more or less, 'if my customers could see where the van actually is, the outage would've been half as bad.' I don't know if that's true, but that's how he feels.
Okay, let's hold that, because that's like forty percent of today.
Holding it. Just flagging, renewal is January 31st and they're at a hundred and forty-five K.
Can I do pipeline real quick?
Go.

So, pipeline is strong. Genuinely — not sales-strong, actually strong. The big one, obviously, is Harbor & Pine. Four hundred and twenty trucks, regional freight in the Pacific Northwest. About three-ten ARR, which would be our biggest logo by a lot. Decision is October 30th. We're up against RouteWise, who are cheaper — I'll be honest, they're cheaper by a meaningful amount. Marcus Hill, their ops director, is our champion and he's great, he gets it. But the CFO, Dana Whitfield, is the one signing, and we've never been on a call with her.
Never?
Never. Marcus says she reads the summary and decides. So whatever Marcus brings her is what we've got.
And integrations? Last I heard, Elena had questions about the TMS.

Elena's fine. Well — Elena's fine-ish. They run Samsara for telematics, which is easy, we've done that a dozen times. And an old on-prem Oracle TMS, which is less easy. But she's not a blocker, she's just thorough.
Thorough is fine. Oracle on-prem is the part that eats a week.
Sure. Anyway — beyond Harbor & Pine we've got three mid-size grocery deals in late stage, and all three want v3. So GA landing on time matters for them too, not just for the OKR.
Which three?

The two regional grocery chains in Texas, and the parcel fleet in Denver that did the pilot over the summer. Together they're about the same ARR as Harbor & Pine, give or take, but they're three separate signatures, so the risk is spread out. All three asked about v3 timing in the last two weeks. One of them asked about live tracking too, but casually. Not a must-have.

Okay. Good to know it's not just one deal holding up the quarter. Okay. So Q3 in one sentence: v3 works, the outage hurt us with exactly the customer we can't afford to hurt, and the pipeline is real but the biggest deal depends on someone we've never met.
That's bleak. But accurate.

Can I sneak one thing in? On the driver app side, Q3 was mostly research. We did the funnel analysis and nineteen interviews with new drivers. I'll show the numbers in the onboarding section, but the short version is the drop-off is worse than we thought it was.
How much worse?
I'll save it. It's a good reveal.
She's building suspense.
I'm building a narrative, Tom.
Fine, fine. Okay. Moving on.
